title: Archive chooser
description: Pick an action, a compression and a few options, and see the matching `tar`, `zip` or `gzip` command, its file extension and what every part does.
intro: Leave the tool on `tar` and the action on Create, then switch the compression from gzip to bzip2 to xz and watch two things change together: the letter after `-c` and the extension. Next, choose List and Extract and read the note about compression letters. Finally, try the tasks: they use Jonas's sprites, Ada's release and Mira's assets.
takeaways: `tar` only bundles files into one archive. A compression program is a separate step, which `tar` calls for you: `z` is gzip, `j` is bzip2 and `J` is xz. That is why the names are `.tar.gz`, `.tar.bz2` and `.tar.xz`.

One action letter is required: `c` creates, `t` lists and `x` extracts. `f` takes the archive name and comes last in the group, so `tar -czf assets.tar.gz assets/` works and `tar -cfz assets.tar.gz assets/` does not.
`v` is verbose and only prints file names. `-C directory` extracts into another existing directory; `unzip -d directory` does the same and creates it if needed.

`gzip`, `bzip2` and `xz` compress one file and replace it with `file.gz`, `file.bz2` or `file.xz` unless you pass `-k`. `-d` (or `gunzip`, `bunzip2`, `unxz`) decompresses. They never bundle a directory.

ZIP is both: `zip` bundles and compresses in one go, with the archive name first, and `unzip` extracts. For a directory you need `-r`; without it only the empty folder entry is stored. Use ZIP when the receiver runs Windows.
List without unpacking with `tar -tf`, `unzip -l`, `gzip -l` or `xz -l`. GNU `tar` detects the compression when it reads, but a wrong letter, such as `-xzf` on a `.tar.bz2`, fails.

links.title: GNU tar manual: the operations (create, list, extract) and compression options

tasks.text: Jonas's sprites must go to the publisher as one compressed file. The publisher uses Linux and only wants it to be a small `.tar.gz`. Pick the command that creates it.
Ada ships the whole assets folder to a tester who uses Windows. Pick the command that creates a file that opens there without extra tools.
tasks.why: `zip -r assets.zip assets/` makes a ZIP file, which Windows opens natively. The `-r` includes the folder's contents.

tasks.text: Mira received `sprites.tar.bz2` and wants to see which files it holds, without unpacking anything.
tasks.why: `-t` lists, `j` names bzip2 and `f` takes the file. Nothing is written to disk.

tasks.text: Ada archives an old release for the shelf. Nobody opens it often, so size matters more than speed. Pick the command that creates an xz-compressed archive of assets.
tasks.why: xz usually gives the smallest result of the three, but it is the slowest. The capital `J` selects it.

tasks.text: Mira has `assets.tar.gz` and wants its files unpacked, with a compression flag in the command.
tasks.why: `-x` extracts, `z` matches the gzip compression and `f` names the archive.

tasks.text: Jonas wants `level1.txt` compressed on its own, and he wants to keep the original text file next to the result.
tasks.why: `gzip -k level1.txt` writes `level1.txt.gz` and keeps the original. Without `-k` it would delete the original.
